Superseded in part — 3 September 2026. This handbook is still the best narrative account of the pipeline, but four newer documents are authoritative where they disagree: docs/RESULTS_REGISTER.md (every number as quotable / withdrawn / open), docs/METHODS.md (how to drive the codebase), docs/REFERENCES.md (device physics and the exergy bound), and docs/ARCHITECTURE_EVOLUTION.md. Start at docs/START_HERE.md.

Two corrections that matter most here: the extractor platform is a thin film of GaAs or SiN-encapsulated molecular dye — Yb:YLF is not the cold-zone material — and three solver defaults moved on 2–3 September, so an un-flagged run is no longer the recorded catalogue.

Status — 31 August

The leakage curve was never a measurement, and replacing it moved the headline numbers both ways

31 August — the curve every thermal result rests on was eleven hard-coded numbers

Every temperature in this handbook was solved on a leakage-vs-temperature curve that is a pass-through of a lookup table. The eleven McPAT runs it was fitted from differ in exactly one line of XML, and normalised, the result is bit-for-bit CACTI’s hard-coded I_off_n[0][*] array for “16nm DG HP” — ratio 1.000 at all ten common points, maximum deviation 3.8e-6. That array is written in cacti/technology.cc as literals like 1.52e-7/1.5*1.2*1.07: 32 nm numbers times three fudge factors, reused unchanged for 32, 22 and 16 nm.

And its shape is not a device. Back out the local activation energy and it runs 0.016 eV to 1.081 eV — a 69× spread, and not monotone. 0.016 eV is below kT at room temperature; 1.081 eV is essentially the silicon bandgap. Those are different mechanisms, so no single device produces this curve. It is an interpolation, and this project had been treating it as a measurement.

There is now a simulator, and it took a day rather than the feared week. ngspice 47 built from source with OSDI, loading BSIM-CMG compiled from Verilog-A by OpenVAF, evaluates the ASAP7 7 nm FinFET card directly — all ~130 parameters, an absolute current in amps, fitted to nothing. It is a device and that is checked rather than claimed: Ioff = 0.232 nA/µm at 300 K and a subthreshold swing of 61.7 mV/dec against a 59.5 ideal, with BSIM-CMG 110, 111.2.1 and the Xyce-flavoured tree agreeing to 0.37 %. The one real obstacle was not the card: OpenVAF segfaults on every input, including a five-line diode, because it hands LLVM a dangling non-NUL-terminated pointer. One character.

`[!]` The trap was arithmetic, not physics. One 7 nm fin leaks a few picoamps — below what ngspice’s linear solve can resolve — and every current came back an exact multiple of 2−43 A. Simulating a thousand fins and dividing fixes it. At one fin a cold-end point was 70 % wrong and a model-version cross-check appeared to disagree by 10 % where it actually agrees to 0.37 %. That 10 % would have been written up as a model difference.

31 August — and spending it moved two headline numbers in opposite directions

The cold-zone prize is 2.2× bigger than this project’s own curve said. Cooling cache from 350 K to 200 K reduces its leakage 16.6× on the simulated curve and 1.73× on the pipeline one — and the pipeline number is 1.73× at every cold temperature, because that curve clamps below 300 K. The clamp was read as a floor for the whole cold-zone argument; it is simply where CACTI’s table stops. The prize was recorded as the largest uncertainty in the architecture case, 13.5 % of die power against the book’s 31.7 %; the answer is the book’s end of that range.

Quote the 2.2×, not a percentage. Converting to “% of die power” needs a static fraction and a cache share, and the recorded pair could not be reproduced from any trace in this repository — the two candidate pairs give 10 % and 30 %. The 2.2× improvement is identical under both, because both multiply the same 1 − 1/reduction by a constant. Re-deriving those two ratios is an open item.

`[+]` And the prize saturates at roughly 280 K. Below that, another 80 K of cooling buys under 5 % more. The design target is barely sub-ambient, not cryogenic — a far easier machine than the reduction factors suggest. The book’s “realistic 100–200×” is about 6× too big and it does not matter: 16.6× already collects 94 % of what 200× would. Quote the die power, never the reduction factor.

`[!]` The density ceiling moved the other way, and the prediction was backwards. The reasoning had been: the pipeline’s Arrhenius tail is far too steep, a gentler tail runs away later, therefore the flat-die ceiling of 1.0–1.2 W/mm² is conservative. Measured on the simulated curve, the uniform arm now fails at 1.00 W/mm² where it previously held at 65.99 °C — one rung lower, resolved by the solver’s own guard as a genuine runaway rather than a damping artefact. The “conservative” claim is withdrawn; the recorded ceilings are optimistic instead.

Why, and it is the part worth carrying. Thermal runaway is a local instability: it is decided by d(ln Pleak)/dT at the temperature the die is actually sitting at, not by leakage at 500 K — by 500 K it has already run away under either curve, so the 47× disagreement there lives where the answer does not. The surviving points occupy 317–347 K, and in that band the ordering reverses: the pipeline curve is nearly flat (0.0013/K at 310 K — the clamp again) while the simulated one runs ~0.036/K throughout, giving it 9.2× more feedback gain at 320 K. The two cross over near 345 K. More gain runs away earlier.

So the defect that mattered was never the hot tail. A surviving die never reaches 500 K. It is that the curve is nearly flat at 310–330 K, understating feedback gain by roughly an order of magnitude exactly where dies operate — and the same flatness is what made the cold-zone prize look small. One clamp, two wrong answers, in opposite directions, and neither was the error we went looking for.

30 August — the liquid-vs-photonic comparison is withdrawn and replaced

It was scored where the answer cannot matter. The comparison fixed the die at 250 W and enforced no junction limit anywhere, and it swept a single baseline. Both are fatal. Below a cooler’s thermal limit the cheapest pump wins by construction — a cold plate there runs at system COP 20 and nothing competes — so the question only becomes real above it. And the air baseline it compared against sits at 381.2 K = 108 °C, past a 100 °C limit and well past 85 °C: that operating point is illegal, and a result measured there means nothing.

Rebuilt as a rescue — pricing a die its cooler cannot otherwise run — the three mechanisms diverge by their exponents. More airflow goes as P ∝ R−5, so a 900 W die needs a 35.8 kW fan. A sub-ambient chiller has COP = η₂Tin/(Ta−Tin), which collapses as the rescue deepens — system COP 20 → 0.15 across 4× overload. The array’s cost per watt is flat, and its recovery term rises with Th. The contrast is about where each machine is forced to work: the chiller at the coldest point in the system, where its COP is worst and still falling; the array at the hottest, where φ is largest.

`[!]` This does not hand the array the win. Against this repository’s own measured rescue — a 34-core die at 133.8 °C unaided, held at 90.6 °C through the coupled solve — the same rescue by chiller needs only 41.8 K of depth, where COP is still 2.47: 163.8 W of system power against the array’s 230.7 W. The array overtakes past roughly 100 K of depth charged for bulk power, or 112.5 K charged only for the hotspot — 24.5 K once the leakage credit is counted. The rescue framing locates where the win starts; it does not deliver it. Two things it does not price, both favouring the array: a 258 K inlet is far below dew point, so the chiller route needs the enclosure sealed against condensation, and the array creates no sub-ambient surface at all.

`[+]` And the rescue pays for a quarter of itself. Holding that die at 90.6 °C instead of 133.8 °C drops what the chip draws from 124.9 W to 91.7 W — 26.6 %, pure leakage feedback — taking the array from 2.473 W/W gross to 1.683 W/W net. That credit was in the evidence and no ledger had counted it.

30 August — what the array is actually for, stated sharply

Granularity converts spatial structure into efficacy, and nothing else. Measured across the pitch ladder, 2000 µm → 50 µm is worth 1.90× on a concentrated hotspot and 0.69× on a uniform die — that is, nothing. Fine pitch is not a general good. It follows that array value cannot be quoted per die: the same hardware is worth 2.77× more on one shape than another, so it is a property of workload and floorplan rather than of the part.

`[+]` Aimed efficacy is flat, then falls off a cliff, and the cliff has a cause. Holding die, shape, pitch and burial fixed and moving only the budget: efficacy is 1.854 K/W flat from 1 W to 16 W — not a percent of decay across a 16× range — then marginal efficacy drops to 0.133 K/W by 32 W. 16 W is exactly what the target block dissipates. Up to it the target is the die peak; past it another block is, and every further watt aimed at the original target buys almost nothing.

Coarse tiles delay the cliff, substantially, and it still never pays. 50 and 200 µm migrate after 16 W, 500 µm after 24 W, and 2000 µm has not migrated at all by 45 W. The collateral-cooling mechanism is real and large — but the delay is bought with plateau height and fine pitch wins at every budget measured, including 45 W where fine has cliffed to 1.030 K/W and coarse, still aiming, manages 0.899. Choose pitch for efficacy; do not try to buy past a bad power map with tile geometry in either direction.

The rule this gives. Size the plan to level the target with the runner-up, then re-aim rather than spend more. That budget is set by peak_to_runner_up_gap_K — the floorplan metric measured here, found weaker than relative_plateau at predicting cost, and nearly set aside. It is weak at predicting cost and it is exactly the right quantity for sizing a plan.

So the claim to carry. The array is not cheaper cooling — on every bulk comparison run here it loses to a pump. It is the only mechanism that can be aimed, worth having where the die is hotspot-limited, worth more the deeper the rescue because its cost per watt is the only one that does not diverge with depth. Recovery improves that ledger by roughly 2×; it does not carry it.

30 August — the loop model had two errors, and the materials moved

This repository carried two statements of the same photonic loop and they disagreed. MRParams.breakeven_ratio omitted the Carnot factor on the anti-Stokes term, making it the φ → 1 limit — it reported the shipped defaults as a net-generating cooler. The guard that should have caught it tests recovered ≤ gross + heat: that is the first law, and it passes. Nothing was testing the second. Every mr_accounting recovery figure recorded before this date is an upper bound, and the measured 34-core rescue's array cost rises 1.419×, from 1.735 to 2.473 W per watt lifted.

`[!]` A second error, in how the feasibility test was used. v91 (1.16) is ηP·ηcpl·[1 + ηASF·φ] ≥ 1, in which ηLPC has already been eliminated by substituting its exergy ceiling (1.14). Folding it into the coupling term double-counts it. Corrected against the book's own worked Examples 1–3 of §1.12, which the code now reproduces to three figures, the required ηASF at 600 K falls 0.548 → 0.347 and at 400 K 1.062 → 0.672. The earlier claim that every temperature inside McPAT's domain needs ηASF > 1 is withdrawn.

`[+]` ηP is now the binding term, not the extractor. The requirement is [1/(ηPηcpl) − 1]/φ, very steep near unity. At ηASF = 0.30 the self-powering temperature is 716 K at ηP 0.85, 469 K at 0.90 and 358 K at 0.95. §1.12 Example 3 says the same of ηcpl: one 20 % front-end loss roughly doubles the extractor target. The laser and the optical path are the hard part now.

`[!]` Yb:YLF is superseded for compute tiles, and “0.02 demonstrated” should not be quoted. Chapter 8 gives two platforms at 10³–10⁴ W/mm² against Yb:YLF's 1–10 — thin-film semiconductor (GaAs) extractor tiles, and SiN-encapsulated molecular dye thin films which reach the same density at room temperature, solution-processed on any planar substrate, with ηEQE 99 % at Nt ≥ 10⁻² M. Table 8.1 gives ηASF 0.124 at a 680 nm pump rising to 0.221 at 740 nm. Yb:YLF is correctly scoped as the cold-zone material. At ηASF ≥ 0.30 the loop closes inside the 400–600 K hot-compute zone of §10.8.

`[!]` And the consequence that matters most: the device envelope in this handbook is stale by 4–40×. Every result here was computed with a cooling intensity ceiling of 250 W/mm², from the Yb:YLF-era draft. Table 8.2 gives 10³–10⁴ W/mm² for both current platforms, and Figure 1.6 puts hot-spot demand at the same 10³–10⁴ W/mm² — so supply now matches demand where it previously fell short by that factor. This is not a refinement: the rescue study's own solver diagnostic reads “envelope insufficient: dt_max binds … this is the device's temperature lift, not its cost”. The binding constraint in the rescue results was the actuator, and the actuator was understated. Sections quoting a cooling-power ceiling, an MR rescue cost, or a “MR loses” verdict should be read as pending re-run until the envelope is refreshed.

`[+]` And a recorded gap is closed structurally. This handbook listed “ηAS(Th) is not modelled at all” as an open item. §8.4 answers it: a heterogeneous die does not use one extractor across its area — but not by swapping to a rare-earth crystal. Corrected 3 September 2026: an earlier revision of this section listed Yb:YLF/Yb:silica for the cold zone, Yb:ZBLAN warm and Ho³⁺/Tm³⁺ fluorides hot. That material list is withdrawn. The shipping device is a thin film of GaAs or SiN-encapsulated molecular dye, and both cover the cold cache band (GaAs is tabulated to 77 K, the dye to 250 K) and the hot compute band up to 400 K. Above 400 K neither platform is tabulated — that is an open gap, not a licence to reintroduce the rare-earths, and it does not bind today because a die that survives never gets there. What survives from §8.4 is the principle: per-tile temperature targeting requires per-tile extractor selection, because ηASF and the achievable lift both depend on local Tj. The numerical ηASF(T) curve inside each window remains open. See HotGauge.thermal.microrefrigeration.ZONE_EXTRACTORS, whose tests refuse any rare-earth name.

Status — 28 August

The catalogue has been re-run, and the packaging term is most of the effect

28 August — a result in this handbook is retracted

The one floorplan metric that had survived phase 1 does not survive better floorplans. Plateau width against cost ordered six dies at ρ +1.00; rebuilt on published block areas, with everything else held identical, the same regression gives +0.29 / −0.06 / −0.29. All six of the original dies were uniform rescales of one unit mix, so plateau width and die size were never independent variables. The ρ +0.84 across eleven workloads on a single die stands; the claim that it transfers across designs does not.

The same rebuild found the power model’s unit mix disagrees with the one published core decomposition by up to 3.6× per block, and carries a 22 % unallocated slab where a real core has 1.35 %. That slab was acting as a heat spreader: rebuilt on published mixes, the same die area at the same watts runs 7 to 24 K hotter. The absolute temperatures in this handbook are optimistic, and by tens of kelvin rather than a few.

The one result that came out clean. Run at the power densities their vendors publish, on dies of the same area and the same cooler, Arm’s wide-vector Neoverse V1 dissipates 31 W less, runs 19 K cooler and is cheaper to cool than the compact Neoverse N1. Both ends of that comparison are published numbers. It is an activity difference, and it is the first ISA result here that a common-density sweep could not have produced.

One more thing to know before quoting any peak. The hottest block on every die in this project — including the unmodified baseline — is the results broadcast bus, which the power model reports as an area overhead and the tiler places as a rectangle at 105 W/mm². It stands only 0.2–3.9 K above the next block, so it distorts the peak by a few kelvin rather than changing the picture — except on the largest core, where the same block carries nine times the power and the die has no steady state at all. Sections marked rebuilt 28 August carry the corrected work; the sections they supersede are kept and labelled rather than deleted.

Read this before quoting anything below

The re-run is done. The 24 August note said “nothing has been re-run”; 180 CPU points and 72 accelerator points have now been re-solved with the cooling in the pixel array where the hardware puts it, on a corrected boundary, in three arms. Every row carries a placement stamp — 714 of 714, none missing — so a result from this generation can be told from the last one by inspection rather than by date.

The headline moved, and not in the direction anyone was arguing about. Three arms separate what the laser does from what the packaging does, and on the 34-core die the packaging is most of it. Swapping 30 µm of thermal grease for 30 µm of GaAs — with the laser off — moves the thermal cliff from 0.80–0.85 to 0.92–0.96 W/mm², and rescues 80 operating points that have no steady state under grease. Reported as a single “MR delta”, as the two-arm scheme did, that gain would have been credited to the light.

Two corrections behind those numbers. The cold-plate base is now folded into the boundary with its real overhang instead of sitting in the stack as a column the width of the die — as a stack layer it tracked 1/area exactly, 15.5× across the die sizes modelled here, which is why the gate reproduced an 826 mm² accelerator and failed a 91 mm² CPU. And the device envelope was raised from an unsourced 10 W/mm² / 10 K to the demonstrated 250 W/mm² / 45 K. Absolute temperatures from before those corrections are not comparable with these; the arm deltas are.

Every accelerator temperature published before 20 August remains withdrawn, and now for a documented reason: those runs predate the fix that made leakage feedback live on that die, so they are constant-power solves. Geometry results — plateau widths, degeneracy, placement sensitivity — follow from the power map and stand. (The accelerator has since been re-solved on a measured microchannel cold plate; see the accelerator status in the footer for what that restores.)

Do not read a catalogue point's density off its tag. The density grids were re-centred onto the measured cliff but sixteen point names were not: margin_T95_d1.10 ran at 0.80 W/mm², ceiling_d1.17 at 0.95, and cores128_d1.00 at 0.70 — overstating by up to 43%. The density field in the harvested JSON is correct throughout, so this is a naming defect and not a data one: trust the field, not the tag. docs/evidence/catalogue_naming_and_margin_defects.json.

And most of the catalogue's MR plans did nothing. Only 17 of 85 points that build a plan had anything above target to act on; the other 68 returned “nothing above target”, removed zero watts and engaged zero blocks. That is not a failure of the planner — it is the corrected boundary putting the die 12–26 K below targets that were written for the old one. It does mean the cost-of-margin and per-watt-rescue numbers in this handbook have no backing until the targets are re-centred and the study re-run.

An acceptance gate against published parts

Five defects have surfaced in sequence, and none was found by reading code. Each came from comparing against something external. So the comparison is now in the test suite: reference operating points from parts you can buy, run through the same coupled solve every study uses.

Reference pointpublishedmodelverdict
H100 80GB, air, ~470 W arXiv:2507.16781 54–72 °C61.0 °C pass
Ryzen 5 7500F, 360 mm AIO, 129 W 70–71 °C64.2 °C pass*
Ryzen 5 7500F, air, 132 W nhsjs.com/2026 75–76 °Crunaway fail
H100 80GB, direct-to-chip liquid, ~453 W 41–50 °C— fail

2 of 4, re-measured 27 August with the spreading boundary wired. The published resistance is junction-to-ambient and already contains the package, which 3D-ICE then adds again — so external cooling supplies only the remainder, 0.1074 − 0.0542 = 0.0532 K/W on the H100 air point. And the heatsink is sized by cooler class, not by a universal ratio to die area.

The blocking failure is gone, and that is the result — not the score. The Ryzen package was 0.4675 K/W against a 0.3962 K/W total budget: the package alone exceeded the entire junction-to-ambient allowance, leaving a negative share for the cooler. That is impossible rather than mis-tuned, and it is why two points could not be reached at any flow. With the lid and cold plate in the boundary carrying their real overhang it is 0.1223, a 31 % share, and both Ryzen points now have a feasible external budget.

pass* — read the liquid Ryzen pass as the weaker of the two. 64.2 °C against a published 70–71 °C is 5.8 K below the range. That is inside the 8 K acceptance tolerance and a legitimate pass, but its flow solver bottomed out at the minimum flow — the cooler is at the solver floor, so the point says the package no longer eats the budget and says nothing about whether the cooler model is right.

The two remaining failures have different causes and neither is the sink model. The Ryzen air point now fails on a leakage runaway in the coupled solve, at 132 W spread by area over a 14-core Skylake floorplan — which is not a Zen 4 CCD, and distinguishing “the modelled cliff is too low” from “the power map is a stand-in” needs a real floorplan, not a parameter change. The H100 liquid point needs 0.0037 K/W of external resistance after the stack and the spreading have taken their share of a 0.0662 K/W budget, which no flow in the class reaches.

Four package inputs behind this gate remain unvalidated — die-attach solder thickness and conductivity, cold-plate thickness and conductivity — and moving all four favourably is worth −0.228 K/W, which would land Ryzen at 0.385 against a published 0.396. None was touched. Adjusting them until the gate passes is tuning against the acceptance test, which is the failure the gate exists to prevent. They are not four wrong numbers so much as four unsourced ones: they are the upstream skylake.stk values, inherited layer-for-layer, and that file cites nothing for them.

Both failures have one cause, and it is now identified

Reading the stack file back as a resistance budget made it visible at a glance, and the budget cross-checks against the solver itself — 0.0402 K/W predicted against 0.0406 measured on the 826 mm² die, 0.3648 against 0.361 on 91 mm².

package layer826 mm²91 mm² share
solder TIM0.00970.087924%
copper spreader0.00930.084523%
thermal grease0.00910.082423%
sink metal0.00810.073320%
silicon (7 layers)0.00400.036610%
total0.0402 0.3648—

The total scales exactly as 1/area — 9.08× for 9.08× the area — which is the signature of no lateral spreading whatsoever. Every layer spans precisely the die footprint, because 3D-ICE takes its chip dimensions from the floorplan and the template's heat-spreader geometry sits inside a /* REMOVED BECAUSE THEY LIE */ block.

A real integrated heat spreader is roughly 40×40 mm over an 8×8 mm die and carries heat sideways before handing it up. On an 826 mm² die the missing overhang costs little, which is exactly why the accelerator point passes. On 91 mm² the package reaches 0.36 K/W against a 0.396 budget and swamps everything. Direct-to-chip liquid fails from the other side: D2C deletes the lid and spreader, so a lidded package spends the entire budget before the coolant is reached.

It also cleared the material constants, which I had suspected. They are correct once the units are read properly — 3D-ICE quotes conductivity in W/(µm K), so silicon's 1.20e-4 is 120 W/(m K) and grease's 0.04e-4 is 4. Read as SI they look like insulators.

The cooling was in the wrong layer, and that made the burial depth inert

The direct-die rebuild below was the easier half. The harder one: MR was applied as negative power on processor floorplan blocks, and those powers land in the die’s own source layer. Cooling and heating were therefore in the same 20 µm of silicon, and the extracted watt crossed nothing on its way out. That is not a small approximation — it means the burial depth of the active layer could not affect any MR result, by construction, which is precisely the parameter a chip vendor has to agree to.

The array is now its own 3D-ICE die element bonded to the exposed silicon, carrying negative power on a floorplan of pixel tiles. Same stack, same 3 W, only the placement changing:

burial depthno MR MR in the source layerMR in the pixel layer over-stated by
360 µm (unthinned)81.85 °C −8.57 K−4.07 K 2.11×
100 µm76.81 °C −8.47 K−5.66 K 1.50×
20 µm75.93 °C −9.25 K−6.80 K 1.36×
moves across the sweep— 0.78 K, not monotone 2.73 K, +67% —

The last row is the result. With the cooling in the source layer the gain barely moves across a factor of eighteen in burial depth, and what movement there is is not even monotone — it is a changing baseline, not the depth doing anything. With the cooling in the pixels it improves as the die thins. Die thinning is worth something only under the second arrangement, and the first is what the whole back catalogue used.

The 67% is not a die-wide constant — qualify it before quoting

The table above is a block maximum on L3_4, measured by driving 3D-ICE directly. Two things move it several-fold, and both were found by re-running the same experiment through the production path on 26 August:

Block maximum against block average. The probe writes its own stack with Tflp(…, maximum, final). The production path is average — so every catalogue row, and every block the planner ranks on, is a block mean. On the same block at the same depth the two differ by 2.6 K.

Which block. On averages the hottest block is L2_4, not L3_4. The same direct probe re-run on L2_4 gives +11.0 %.

Driven end to end through the planner — same 3 W, same block, byte-identical tile plan at every depth — the swing is +44.1 % in the array against −7.0 % in the source layer. What survives all three measurements is the claim that matters: array placement is strongly burial-sensitive and co-located placement is not. Quote the magnitude with the block and the reduction stated, or quote the separation.

The array also has geometry now. A plan could previously cool a 142 × 13 µm block and nothing else — a pixel pitch of 13 µm. Real tiles are hundreds of microns across and cool whatever is under them; projection is by area overlap and the collateral area is reported rather than hidden.

The package was wrong before it was incomplete

The overhang gap above is real, but it was the second problem. The first is that a solder die attach and a 3 mm copper lid have no business being in this model at all. Photonic microrefrigeration puts a tile array on the silicon; a package that buries the silicon under 3.2 mm of metal and polymer is not the thing being proposed. Together those two layers are 47% of the stack’s resistance, and they sit between the cooler and the heat.

The stack is now generated from a specification rather than kept as a checked-in file, and a direct-die build removes both. The pixel array takes the place the thermal grease occupied, which costs nothing thermally — GaAs at 55 W/(m K) is fourteen times more conductive than the polymer TIM it displaces, so adding the cooler lowers the stack resistance even before it removes a single watt.

 826 mm²91 mm² package share of the published budget, 91 mm²
lidded (every result so far)0.0402 0.364891% — fails
direct die, bare TIM0.02120.1923 49%
direct die + GaAs pixels 0.01280.1159 29% — comparable to the one point that passes
direct die + Si₃N₄ pixels0.0133 0.120931%

A 68% cut, identical at both die sizes because every layer is still 1/area. On the 91 mm² part that moves the package from 91% of the published junction-to-fluid budget to 29% — from “no flow can supply the remainder” to roughly where the accelerator point sits when it passes. Whether the gate actually passes is a re-run, not a claim: these are lumped 1-D budgets, and the solve is the arbiter.

Two things fall out of the rebuild that are worth recording separately.

The active layer’s depth is now a parameter. Under direct die there is nothing above the transistors but silicon and the pixels, so how deep they are buried decides the answer — and it is set by how thin a vendor will grind the wafer, not by us. examples/burial_depth_sweep.py produces the curve that conversation needs. Every point in it is a new system matrix, so nothing shares a factorisation.

3D-ICE mis-parses banner comments. Its scanner skips "*"[^/] — two characters at a time — so a run of * before a comment’s closing / is consumed in pairs and the comment only terminates when that run is odd. An even run swallows the rest of the file, and the parse error surfaces at whatever section keyword comes next, nowhere near the cause. The historical templates survive this by luck: every banner in skylake.stk happens to have 23 trailing stars. The generator emits no block comments at all and refuses to write one that would trip it.

Fixing it inside 3D-ICE: two of three obstacles cleared

A real spreader exists in 3D-ICE, but only on the pluggable sink model, and upstream refuses that in steady state with a bare //TODO. That TODO understates it. Three things stand in the way:

  • fixed The steady vector fill walked only the chip layers, so the spreader rows were never written.
  • fixed The plugin computes heat flow from the temperature it is handed, so one linear solve cannot close it. Now a fixed point — the same shape as the leakage feedback one level up.
  • open Spreader cells have no conductance to ambient. The plugin contributes heat as a source, never as a matrix coefficient. In transient the capacity/timestep term on the diagonal keeps the system non-singular; in steady it is zero, so the matrix is singular — a pure Neumann problem with no reference temperature anywhere. SuperLU returns NaN.

The remedy is to linearise the plugin into the matrix rather than the right-hand side: probe it at two uniform temperatures to recover g and Tambient from Q = g(T − Tambient), then add g to the spreader diagonal. For a linear boundary that is exact, needs no iteration, and preserves the factorisation so the session cache still works.

Until then the path detects the singularity and explains it, rather than iterating on NaN or handing back a plausible field.

Re-run — 27 August

What the three arms separated, and what moved

Every earlier MR number in this document compared two things: the die with cooling and the die without. That comparison cannot distinguish the laser from the packaging, because the array is 30 µm of GaAs standing where 30 µm of thermal grease used to be, and GaAs conducts about fourteen times better. The re-run uses three arms — control (grease, no cooling), array_idle (GaAs at zero optical power) and array_on (GaAs under the planner) — so the two terms are reported separately. On this die, at these densities, the packaging term is the larger one.

The cliff moves before the laser is switched on

34-core, 88 CFM, 500 µm pitch, 200 µm burial, spreading boundary. Peak junction temperature against die-average power density:

W/mm²control (grease)array_idle (GaAs, 0 W) passive gain
0.3044.2 °C41.5 °C2.7 K
0.4556.4 °C52.3 °C4.1 K
0.6068.6 °C63.1 °C5.5 K
0.7076.7 °C70.3 °C6.4 K
0.8084.9 °C77.5 °C7.4 K
0.85RUNAWAY 81.1 °C—
0.88RUNAWAY83.3 °C —
0.92RUNAWAY86.2 °C —
0.96RUNAWAY RUNAWAY—

Two cliffs, cleanly separated. Under grease the die loses its steady state between 0.80 and 0.85 W/mm². With the unpowered array it survives to between 0.92 and 0.96. That is a 14 % density gain from a materials substitution, with the laser off — and across the whole 180-point re-run it rescues 80 operating points that have no steady state under grease.

The passive term grows from 2.7 K at 0.30 W/mm² to 7.4 K at 0.80, and to 33.4 K at the densities where the control is nearly unstable. It is not a fixed offset: a modest conductivity gain becomes tens of kelvin near the cliff, because that is where leakage feedback is steepest. Under the old two-arm scheme all of that would have been reported as a photonic result.

Where the laser does the work

Across the re-run, 45 points had something above the MR target for the planner to act on. There the laser removes 0.04–124.7 W and buys a further 0.3–50.2 K on top of the passive term. The top of that range only exists because the device envelope was corrected: dt_max was an unsourced 10 K and is now the demonstrated 45 K, so a 50 K result was previously clipped by an assumption rather than by physics.

The optimal granularity reverses with the workload — re-measured on the full ladder

Swept over 50 / 100 / 200 / 500 / 1000 / 2000 µm at a fixed 3 W removal budget:

power mapbestworstspread on the same 3 W
uniform — degenerate peak 2000 µm (coarsest) 2.93 K 500 µm, 2.00 K0.94 K
concentrated — isolated hotspot per-block (finest) 5.57 K 2000 µm, 2.93 K2.63 K

The coarsest array is the best choice on a degenerate peak and the worst on a concentrated one. One tile spanning several plateau members clips them together, which per-block cooling cannot do at any price; the same tile over an isolated hotspot spends most of its watts on silicon that was already cool. Which regime a die is in is a property of its power map, not of the cooler.

The second column matters as much as the first: the concentrated case swings 2.63 K across the ladder against 0.94 K for the uniform one. A coarse array is low-variance and a fine one is not — which is a manufacturing and control-loop argument, and it exists only as a comparison across the ladder. A single fixed pitch reports a curve as a number and loses both results.

What is not comparable with the older numbers

Absolute temperatures. The cold-plate base moved out of the stack, where 3D-ICE gave it exactly the die footprint, and into the boundary with its real overhang. On the 34-core die that changes the boundary the die sees from 0.0764 to 0.3247 K/W, and it is die-size dependent where the old one was not: 0.55 K/W on a 28 mm² die against 0.11 on an 826 mm² one, where before it was a flat 0.0764 on both. Small dies get hotter and the cliff moves down with them.

Arm deltas are comparable, which is why the pitch stayed at the back-catalogue 500 µm for every fixed-pitch point: moving the boundary and the granularity at once would have left nothing that could be compared with anything.

Accelerator temperatures published before 20 August stay withdrawn. They predate the fix that made leakage feedback live on that die and are constant-power solves. Separately, the accelerator needed a real cold plate: the finned water block the model had been using gives 0.055 K/W and the GA100 has no steady state above ~250 W on it, while a direct-die microchannel plate anchored on a measured reference gives 0.0153 K/W and the same die runs 51.4 °C at 400 W and 64.0 °C at 700 W.

01 — The question

Can you cool a processor with light, and is it worth doing?

Maxwell Labs is developing photonic microrefrigeration (MR): a solid-state cooler that removes heat from a chip using anti‑Stokes fluorescence. A laser pumps a crystal bonded to the die; the crystal re-emits light at a shorter wavelength than it absorbed, and the energy difference comes out of the lattice as heat. The re-emitted light is carried away, and some of it is recovered as electricity by a photovoltaic cell (the “LPC”). The result is a cooler with no moving parts that can be aimed at a spot on the die roughly ten microns across.

That last property is the interesting one. Conventional cooling — a heatsink, a fan, a cold plate — removes heat from the whole package. MR can remove it from one block. The premise of the project is that this ought to be worth a great deal, because a processor’s limits are usually set by its hottest structure rather than its average temperature.

This work exists to test that premise quantitatively, and to say where it holds. The concrete deliverable is not a yes or no; it is a set of numbers a device team can aim at and a system architect can plan around.

What we are actually simulating

A processor die under a real workload, solved for its steady-state temperature field with temperature-dependent leakage in the loop — hotter silicon leaks more current, which makes it hotter still. We then add microrefrigeration to selected blocks and re-solve, and compare against the alternative of simply buying more conventional cooling.

02 — The physics, in one page

Four mechanisms explain nearly every result here

1. Leakage–temperature feedback, and thermal runaway

Transistor leakage rises steeply with temperature. Power heats the die, the die leaks more, the extra leakage is more power. At low density this converges to a steady state. Above some density it does not: the loop diverges and the part has no steady state at all. That threshold — the stability cliff — is at 0.80–0.85 W/mm² on our CPU die with 88 CFM of air, under conventional thermal grease. Substituting the GaAs pixel array for that grease — with the laser off — moves it to 0.92–0.96. (Both re-measured 27 August on the corrected spreading boundary; the pre-correction figure was 1.05–1.10 and is superseded throughout.)

This matters because runaway is a local phenomenon driven by the hottest blocks, and MR is a local tool. Arresting a runaway turns out to be extraordinarily cheap.

2. Constriction resistance

Heat leaving a small hot block has to spread through silicon before it reaches the heatsink. That spreading resistance is a property of the die, not of the cooler, so no amount of airflow removes it. We measure it as β − α ≈ 1.04 K/W, essentially flat from 88 to 600 CFM. It is why spinning the fan harder eventually stops helping a hotspot while continuing to cost power.

3. Thermal degeneracy — the plateau

If many blocks sit at nearly the same temperature, cooling the hottest one achieves almost nothing, because the second-hottest immediately becomes the peak. We call the set of blocks within the device’s reach of the peak the plateau, and its width is the single strongest predictor of whether hotspot cooling can help. A balanced CPU die has 15 blocks in its plateau. A uniformly loaded accelerator has 332 of 367.

4. Depth versus breadth

A cooler is limited in two independent ways: how many blocks it can cover, and how far down it can pull any one of them. These are different constraints with different fixes, and confusing them wasted a week of this project. Breadth is the plateau; depth is dt_max.

03 — Glossary

Terms, defined precisely

Several of these look like they should be related and are not. The distinctions matter enough that mixing them up has produced wrong conclusions in this project more than once.

clip‑one gain

How many kelvin the die’s peak temperature falls if you apply the cooler to exactly one block — the hottest one — and pull it down as far as the device allows.

It is a measure of degeneracy, not of the cooler. If the second-hottest block is 0.04 K below the peak, then removing the peak block entirely lowers the die by 0.04 K and no further, however good the cooler is. So clip-one gain answers: is there a hotspot here worth aiming at?

We report it against the device’s own capability. “0.040 K, 0.4% of the device” means the cooler could have delivered 10 K of lift and the die’s structure only let 0.04 K of it turn into a lower peak.

A caution learned the hard way: clip-one gain is the right metric when the plateau is wide and you cannot afford to cool all of it. When the plateau collapses to a handful of blocks, the relevant question becomes the cost of cooling the whole plateau, and clip-one understates MR badly. We drew a wrong conclusion from it once.

dt_max — “a 10 K device”

The maximum temperature lift the refrigerator can sustain: how many kelvin colder than its surroundings it can hold the spot it is cooling. Our baseline device is 10 K. This is a thermodynamic property of the cooler.

It is not the COP, and in our model the two are entirely independent. A block sitting 12.6 K above where you need it cannot be rescued by a 10 K device at any efficiency, however cheap the watts are. That is a hard wall, and it is the wall we are currently against.

h_max

Maximum cooling power density the stage can deliver, 10 W/mm². How much heat per unit area, as distinct from how deep a temperature drop. In practice this has never been the binding constraint in our runs — the plans we compute use a few percent of it.

COP, and its three flavours

Coefficient of performance — watts of heat removed per watt spent. We track three, and conflating them overstates the cooler:

  • ηASF = 0.20 — optical COP: heat removed per watt of light delivered to the crystal.
  • Electrical COP = 0.14 — ηASF × ηlaser (0.70 wall-plug). Heat removed per watt drawn from the wall.
  • Effective COP = 0.574 — after the LPC recovers 76% of the draw as electricity. This is the figure that belongs in a system power budget.

There is also a device break-even: if the recovery ratio exceeds 1, the loop returns more power than it draws. At our laser and LPC efficiencies that needs ηASF ≥ 0.587 — so the extractor, not the LPC, is the binding term there.

plateau

The number of blocks within dt_max of the peak temperature. Equivalently: how many blocks you would have to cool to realise the device’s full lift. Wide plateau ⇒ hotspot cooling is structurally the wrong tool. Narrow plateau ⇒ it may be exactly the right one.

rescue vs. holding a temperature

Two different questions that our tooling can both answer, and that we mislabelled for weeks:

Rescue — the cheapest plan that gives a runaway die any steady state. It lands wherever the stable branch happens to sit.

Holding a target — the cheapest plan that pins the peak to a stated temperature. It requires cooling everything between the target and the peak, which on a degenerate die is the entire plateau.

The distinction is the point, and it is structural. On the superseded boundary the two were measured on the same die at the same nominal 98 °C and came out 450× apart — 0.29 W to rescue, 131 W to hold. Those two numbers are withdrawn: they were taken at 1.10 W/mm², which is now far past the cliff, and the re-centred margin study returns nothing to re-measure them with (see “Cost is dominated by how much margin you demand”). The ratio has not been re-measured. The instruction stands regardless: always quote which one you mean, and the achieved peak alongside the watts.

volumetric extraction, and R = 0

The claim that distinguishes photonic cooling from every conventional technology, and the one worth being precise about. Conventional cooling removes heat through a surface, so it always pays the conduction path from the hotspot outwards. MR couples to phonons inside the silicon, so the extracted heat never travels that path at all.

The MR writeup (§3.6.5) puts it as cancelling “any conduction-induced thermal resistance, thereby setting R = 0 between any hotspot and the working fluid”, with its Table 10 giving laser cooling Rth,hotspot = 0, independent of area, where air is 20–50 and liquid 5–10 K·cm²/W and both worsen as the hotspot shrinks.

Follow it to its conclusion and there is a fixed point: when extraction per unit area matches dissipation per unit area the net source is zero and no heat flows, so the effective resistance is zero; push extraction higher and the block goes below its surroundings and heat flows inward — a negative effective resistance at the interface between the cooled layer and the active silicon.

Our model represents this correctly in kind, which was not by design and is worth recording: MR is applied by subtracting power at the source layer, and the subtraction is not clamped at zero. So extracted heat never flows through the stack, and a block can go net-negative. What the model does not yet do is let dt_max be anything other than a hard cap on lift, which is a device constraint rather than the path-bypass the theory describes.

direct die, and burial depth
A conventional processor package puts a solder die attach, a copper lid and a polymer TIM between the silicon and the cooler. Direct die removes the lid and the die attach, so the cooler touches the silicon. Photonic microrefrigeration is only buildable this way — a pixel array on the far side of 3 mm of copper is not cooling the transistors, it is cooling the lid.

Burial depth is then the number that matters: how much silicon sits between the exposed die surface and the active layer. In the historical stack it was 360 µm and it was not adjustable; it is now a parameter (source_depth_um), because it is set by how thin a vendor is willing to grind the wafer and that is a manufacturing and warranty question before it is a thermal one. It also bounds the IP claim: if the benefit is flat from 360 µm down to 30 µm the scheme does not depend on aggressive thinning, and if it is steep the claim is tied to a thinning process.
where the cooling is applied, and why it is the whole question
Microrefrigeration used to be applied by apply_cooling_to_trace as negative power on processor floorplan blocks. Floorplan power lands in the die’s own source layer — the same 20 µm of silicon the transistors occupy — so cooling and heating were co-located and the extracted watt crossed no silicon at all. Under that arrangement sweeping the burial depth moves material no heat flows through on its way to the cooler, so it cannot change the answer. Not approximately: by construction.

The array is now its own 3D-ICE die element bonded to the exposed silicon, with a floorplan of pixel tiles carrying negative power (mr_powered). A watt made in the transistors has to climb the burial depth and cross the bond before anything removes it. Measured, same stack and same 3 W: the old placement over-states what the cooling buys by 2.11× on an unthinned die, 1.50× at 100 µm, 1.36× at 20 µm — and it never converges, because even on a 20 µm die the watt still crosses the bond.

The array also has geometry now, which the old formulation could not express at all. A plan could previously cool a 142 × 13 µm block and nothing else, which is a pixel pitch of 13 µm. Real tiles are hundreds of microns across and cool whatever sits under them. Projection is by area overlap, and coverage_report reports the collateral: the die area sitting under an engaged tile, over the area the plan asked to cool.
damping verification

Every result is re-solved at half the numerical damping; if the two disagree, the point is marked unquotable. This is not ceremony — it retired four published figures in a single day. A converged-looking number from an unconverged solve is the characteristic failure mode of this kind of simulation.

system matrix, and why it governs runtime

The thermal solver factorises a sparse matrix built from the stack geometry and the floorplan — not from the power values. So sweeping power, workload, MR target or dt_max reuses one factorisation and is nearly free; sweeping airflow, grid, or die geometry costs a full factorisation each. At accelerator scale that is 431 seconds apiece, and it is the whole of our compute budget.

04 — The dies

Two processors, same node class

Everything is modelled at 7 nm so the two can be compared directly. They are deliberately opposite in structure, which is what makes the comparison informative.

 CPU dieAccelerator die
Basis Skylake-derived floorplan, scaled to 34 cores Nvidia GA100 (A100), from published die analysis
Area101.2 mm² (12.36 × 8.19 mm) 826 mm² (32.39 × 25.50 mm)
Blocks1126367
Structure 34 cores, each with distinct functional units of differing power density 128 near-identical SM tiles, 96 L2 tiles, 6 HBM PHY, 4 memory controllers
Power source Sniper → McPAT, Linpack at 3.8 GHz, per-block Total die power divided by an assumed per-class split
Density studied0.80–1.00 W/mm² (was 1.00–1.17) 0.48 W/mm² at 400 W; 0.85 at 700 W
Fails byThermal runaway — loses its steady state Exceeding its temperature limit while remaining stable

That last row is a structural result rather than a detail. An 826 mm² die spreads heat laterally far better than a 101 mm² one, and dilutes the leakage feedback across eight times the area, so the local positive feedback that destabilises the CPU never closes. The accelerator does not run away where the CPU does — it simply gets too hot. Those need different interventions.

How the accelerator floorplan was built

From annotated die photographs (SemiAnalysis / Locuza): die area, TPC and L2 tile areas, PCIe PHY area, and the physical arrangement are all read off the shots. One number came from a second die (GA102): the SRAM fraction inside a compute tile, 33.4%. Without it the finest structure on the die would be a whole 3.4 mm² SM, and no hotspot smaller than that could exist by construction.

The die outline is fixed by measured area and aspect; the tile height by the measured 16-tall arrangement; the tile width by the tile’s own measured area. The interior width that results is therefore a prediction of the arrangement, not a fit — and it closes on the measured die area.

What the thermal grid can and cannot resolve

This now bites twice. A block thinner than a thermal cell cannot carry its own temperature, and it cannot be cooled in isolation either — the cooling tile above it is on a pitch of hundreds of microns.

3D-ICE discretises the die into square cells — 100 µm on the accelerator, 50 µm on the CPU. A floorplan block thinner than a cell cannot carry its own temperature; it inherits the cell’s. On the accelerator this never bites, because the smallest block is 600 µm across. On the CPU it bites often.

This is the most important table in the document. Nothing here is calibrated against a physical microrefrigerator, because none has been measured into this pipeline yet — so no absolute number in this project is a product prediction. What the model does support are comparisons, where a shared assumption cancels.

It is an interpolation, not a characterisation. The tail decides whether a point diverges, not by how much.
