The assumption most likely to change a conclusion

Our model lets you raise dt_max from 10 K to 13 K without paying anything in efficiency. Real refrigerators do not work that way — COP falls as the temperature lift rises.

We can bound how much that matters, because the efficiency margin is enormous: at the operating point below, MR beats its alternative by 33.7×. So COP could degrade by up to 33.7× between 10 and 13 K before the conclusion flips — a 30% increase in lift causing a 3,000% collapse in efficiency, which no plausible device does. The recommendation survives, but the coupling should be modelled before anyone commits silicon to it.

06 — Analysis modes

What questions the pipeline can actually answer

Any of the variables below can be made the output rather than the input. The two directions asked about most often — constrain performance and solve for efficiency, or constrain efficiency and solve for performance — are both supported, though one of them only for a temperature target rather than a throughput target.

QuestionToolStatus
Given a cooling solution, what clock can the part sustain? clock_headroom.py exercised
Given a temperature target, what COP does MR need to beat more airflow? cop_breakeven.py exercised
Given an efficiency and an MR budget, what clock results? clock_headroom.py --mr --mr-budget-W --eta-asf exercised
Given a fixed cooling power budget, what fan/MR split maximises throughput? hybrid_cooling_optimizer.py (mode A) built, never run
Given a performance target, what is the cheapest cooling and its split? hybrid_cooling_optimizer.py (mode B) built, never run
Given a device lift, what becomes reachable and at what cost? --dt-max-K sweep exercised
How degenerate is this die, and where are its hot blocks? thermal_tiers.py, accelerator_study.py exercised
What does an MR rescue cost at a given density? mr_comparison.py exercised
Given a throughput target, what COP is required? chain clock_headroom → cop_breakeven gap — not automated

The one genuine gap is the last row. cop_breakeven.py solves for efficiency against a temperature constraint; converting a throughput target into the temperature that delivers it requires a separate clock search, and nothing chains the two. It is a modest piece of work and it is the most useful next addition, because throughput is the constraint a customer actually states.

The hybrid_cooling_optimizer is the other opportunity: it already implements both directions of the budget/performance trade and has never been run. Its premise is sound — the fan’s marginal value collapses about 90× across its range while MR’s cost stays roughly linear, and diminishing returns against linear cost is exactly the shape that produces an interior optimum rather than an all-fan or all-MR answer.

07 — Findings

Where microrefrigeration pays, and where it does not

Ordered by how confident we are, most confident first.

MR arrests thermal runaway extremely cheaply mechanism stands density superseded — 27 August

A 34-core die at 1.10 W/mm² has no steady state — left alone it runs away. 0.29 W of net electrical power, applied to four blocks, gives it one, landing just under its 100 °C limit. That is 290 W of die stabilised per watt spent.

Runaway is driven by a handful of blocks, and a local tool is exactly right for a local instability — that reasoning is untouched. The density is not. On the corrected boundary 1.10 W/mm² is far past the cliff rather than just over it, and the catalogue's re-centred grid does not reach it. What replaces the old number is a larger claim and one the three arms let us attribute properly: the grease control loses its steady state at 0.80–0.85 W/mm² and the unpowered GaAs array at 0.92–0.96 — a 14% density gain from a materials substitution, with the laser switched off, and 80 rescued operating points across the run. The per-watt rescue cost has to be re-measured before it is quoted again; see the margin section below for why the study that measured it currently returns nothing.

MR is weak as a clock enabler superseded — 25 August

On the same die, raising the sustainable clock is a different matter: +1.1% for about a watt, +2.2% for 43 W. The clock ceiling is set by the die-average thermal path, which hotspot clipping barely touches. A 50× better heatsink buys +55% clock and still never reaches the part’s rated frequency.

What was wrong with it

Both premises are correct. The clock ceiling is set by the die-average path, and hotspot clipping does barely touch it. The conclusion does not follow, because hotspot clipping is one spatial strategy among several and it is the one that saturates soonest — and it was the only one the pipeline could express, because MR was applied as negative power on individual blocks.

How to move the die-average path: match extraction to dissipation measured

Four spatial strategies at equal total removal, same die, same power, same array. The metric is peak reduction per watt removed, because the peak is what sets the clock:

strategy3 W10 W 30 Wbehaviour
hotspot — all of it on the hottest block0.665 0.4360.235 saturates: −64.7%
top 5 hottest blocks1.119 0.4190.218 saturates: −80.5%
uniform over the die0.3170.317 0.317linear
proportional to the power map0.412 0.4120.412 linear
\n

Two rules fall out, and they are the useful part. Targeted cooling is for small budgets; proportional extraction is for large ones. Cooling the top few blocks is the most efficient thing to do at small budgets; above the crossover, matching extraction to the power map wins and keeps winning, because it has no ceiling to run into. On the re-measured table the crossover sits between 10 and 30 W on this die — at 10 W the top-5 strategy still leads, 0.419 against 0.412, and by 30 W it has fallen to 0.218. Three sampled budgets cannot place it more precisely than that, and the earlier “roughly 7 W” was an interpolation the data did not support.

And proportional extraction is, to a good approximation, just reducing the die power. Removing a fraction f of the heat where it is made moves the peak almost exactly as if the die dissipated (1−f) of its power — re-measured on the corrected boundary, predicted 78.85 / 75.32 / 65.25 °C at 3 / 10 / 30 W against a measured 79.12 / 76.24 / 68.01. The residual is the array’s own resistance and the burial depth beneath it. That is precisely the die-average lever the superseded claim said was out of reach: the heat is taken out before the bottleneck, so every block benefits and nothing over-cools.

This one got stronger when it was re-run

Both sides of that comparison moved when the boundary was corrected — every absolute temperature did. The residuals did not. They come back +0.27 / +0.92 / +2.76 K, matching the superseded measurement to two decimal places, across a boundary that differs by 4.25× in K/W and a burial depth that was half. So the residual is a property of the array layer — its own resistance and the silicon buried beneath it — and not of the sink. A number that reproduces across a change of that size is evidence about the mechanism rather than a coincidence of calibration. docs/evidence/proportional_equals_power_reduction.json.

What this does and does not settle

It refutes the mechanism the old claim rested on. It does not yet give a new clock number — that needs the sustainable-clock search re-run through the array, which is on the list. At the target efficiencies (ηASF 0.33, laser 0.80, LPC 0.87, effective COP 3.55) the arithmetic is 30 W removed for 8.45 W electrical, buying 12.3 K of peak — 1.46 K per electrical watt, independent of budget (1.463 at 3 W, 1.462 at 10, 1.461 at 30). Whether that converts into clock at the rate the old model assumed is the open question.

Which floorplans microrefrigeration suits, measured rather than asserted new 27 August

The project has carried a list of five “phase 1 floorplan metrics” since the architecture ladder was written, together with a rule: regress measured MR benefit against them, and drop any metric that does not predict. It had never been runnable, for a reason nobody had looked for. The eleven workload shapes that give the metrics their variety existed only in control-arm screens with no cooling measured on them; and all 35 catalogue points that did have a measured benefit ran at uniform activity on one die. The predictors and the response had never been measured on the same points.

Thirty-three points later — eleven shapes × three demanded margins — they have. The first thing it settled is that the obvious response variable is wrong. Benefit in kelvin correlates 0.956 with the margin you asked for, because the planner holds the target by construction. Benefit is an input. The response that means anything is cost: the heat you must remove to buy that margin.

metricvs cost, 3 K5 K 8 Kverdict
plateau width, as a fraction of the die's own span +0.843+0.825 +0.852keep — lead with it
die temperature span−0.655 −0.682−0.736 promote — it was only stamped as context
peak-to-runner-up gap−0.682 −0.682−0.582 (p = 0.06) keep, but demote

Spearman ρ, n = 11 shapes at each margin. The plateau metric predicts cost at every margin with consistent sign and magnitude. The peak-to-runner-up gap sees only the top two blocks, and loses significance exactly where the plan is pushed down into the plateau — which is the regime it was meant to describe.

And a split that neither of these metrics predicts

Efficiency retained as the demanded margin grows from 3 K to 8 K divides the eleven shapes almost binarily: six retain 98–100 %, five retain 37–54 %, with essentially nothing in between. It is not ordered by plateau width — two of the widest-plateau shapes scale gracefully while a narrow one collapses to 43 %.

The third metric: how deep the hot region goes built and validated 27 August

The split says what the missing metric has to measure — not how wide the plateau is, but how fast temperature falls below the peak. Neither existing metric can see that: the peak-to-runner-up gap looks at the top two blocks, and the plateau counts blocks rather than measuring a slope.

hot_region_depth is the drop from the peak to the coolest of the hottest 5 % of blocks — a share of blocks rather than a count, so it transfers across floorplans. On the same eleven shapes it separates the two groups cleanly:

metricdegrades groupholds group separation
hot-region depth10.1–14.0 K 19.5–33.0 K clean — a 5.5 K gap, no overlap
plateau widthoverlapping fails — overlaps by 30 blocks, in the wrong direction
peak-to-runner-up gapoverlapping fails — overlaps by 1.8 K, not significant

The mechanism is legible: as the demanded margin grows, the plan must reach further down the distribution. Where temperature falls away steeply below the top few per cent there is a well-defined hot group and cooling stays efficient; where it falls away shallowly the plan meets an ever-widening set of near-peak blocks and efficiency collapses. The split survives cleanly from a 2 % share to a 20 % share, so the 5 % default is not delicate.

Tested across six floorplans the next day — and dropped

It does not transfer. Correlation with retained efficiency is +0.800 across eleven workloads on one floorplan and −0.886 across six floorplans. The sign reverses, and normalising by die span does not rescue it (+0.718 against −0.829). By this handbook's own rule — any metric that does not predict is dropped — it goes, one day after it was built.

The likely reason is worth keeping. Across floorplans this quantity mostly tracks the die's absolute temperature scale, which is set by area and power rather than by the shape of the distribution; within one floorplan the span is roughly fixed and it does measure shape. It survives as a within-floorplan workload diagnostic and must not be used to compare designs. The function is kept, documented and tested as failing, because a metric that fails cleanly is worth more on the record than one quietly deleted.

And it is not alone. relative_plateau reverses too when regressed against retained efficiency (−0.647 on workloads, +0.829 on floorplans). So saturation behaviour appears not to be predictable from the temperature distribution alone by any of these metrics — it seems to need the absolute thermal scale as well. Only plateau-against-cost survives.

Which leaves the scoreboard clean, and short. Of five candidate floorplan metrics, exactly one predicts across both kinds of variation: plateau width, as a fraction of the die's own span, against the cost of holding a margin — ρ +0.84 across eleven workloads, +1.00 across four floorplans, +1.00 across six. Three independent datasets, two kinds of variation, consistent throughout. The others are either dropped or demoted.

Superseded 28 August — the transfer does not survive better floorplans. Every floorplan in those four- and six-die sets was a uniform rescale of one unit mix, so plateau width and die size were never independent variables. Rebuilt on published block areas, where mix and size move separately, the same regression gives +0.29 / −0.06 / −0.29. The +0.84 across eleven workloads on one die stands; what fails is the claim that it transfers across designs. See What the published areas changed below.

What this could not test. It varied the workload, not the floorplan — one die throughout. The two geometric metrics, power-density concentration and hot-block distance to the die edge, were therefore constant across all 33 points and remain completely untested. They need floorplan variants, which is what the ARM and RISC‑V work will supply.

Four ISAs, and a prediction that failed usefully new 27 August

This section records the 27 August cut, which has since been rebuilt. Two of its claims did not survive: the vector scaling described below was declared but never installed — every one of these six dies carries the x86 AVX‑512 block at full size — and the areas are press-derived where published ones now exist. It is kept because the prediction it registered, and the way that prediction failed, are still the cleanest part of the story. The corrected work is What the published areas changed.

Until recently every floorplan in this project was one microarchitecture. There are now six, built by re-weighting the unit mix and handing it to the same tiler. The two that matter most are anchored on published microarchitecture rather than press area ratios: a Fujitsu A64FX-class die — Fugaku silicon, 512-bit SVE, 64 KB L1 each way and 8 MB L2 per 12-core group — and a XiangShan Kunminghu-class die, the open server-class out-of-order RV64 core from ICT/CAS. Their SRAM scaling is derived from real cache capacity against this project's own McPAT configuration, and their vector scaling from real vector width, so core area is an output rather than an assumption.

The open RISC‑V core lists were checked and did not serve: they are overwhelmingly 32-bit in-order embedded and educational parts, with CVA6 as their ceiling at roughly Cortex‑A55 tier. Building an HPC floorplan on one would have been worse than a press ratio, because it would carry the authority of real synthesisable RTL while representing the wrong class of machine. The ISA argument had to be restated first. In this model the instruction decoder is 3.3 % of core area, so “x86 decode is complex” cannot carry an architecture result. What can is where the rest of the area went: vector width — the x86 baseline carries an AVX‑512 accelerator at 1.98× the base FPU area — and core size at constant power.

A prediction was registered before the solves, so that it could fail: a compact core should have a narrower plateau, a wide-vector core should stand further clear of its runner-up, and both should therefore be better MR targets than x86.

It failed on all three counts

Compact dies came out wider-plateaued and more uniform, not narrower — plateau 17 → 71 blocks and span 30.5 → 16.0 K as the core shrinks. And they are more expensive to cool, not less: holding 3 K of margin costs 0.49 W on x86 against 1.35 W on the most compact die, a factor of 2.7 the wrong way.

The error was mine and it is instructive. The reasoning assumed constant die power — less SRAM per watt to buffer the heat. The sweep holds constant density, so a smaller die simply dissipates less: unaided peaks fall 63.1 → 42.9 °C. A cooler die is a flatter die. The confound was built into the experiment by holding the wrong quantity fixed.

And this is why the sweep was worth running. The metric did not fail with the prediction. relative_plateau ordered the cost perfectly — ρ = +1.000 at every one of the three margins. It had already predicted cost at ρ +0.84 across eleven workloads on one die; it now predicts it across four floorplans at one workload. That answers the question the workload regression could not: a predictor validated on eleven workloads might merely have been describing that floorplan, and it was not. A metric that survives its own designer's prediction being wrong is better evidence than one that agrees with it.

Which is why the experiment was repeated at constant power

Those variants re-weight area, with the power trace redistributed over it at constant density — so what the sweep above measured is that smaller dies at constant density run cooler and flatter, which is nearly a tautology once said plainly. The prediction was about constant power. So it was run again, holding total watts fixed and letting density follow from die area.

At constant power, half the sweep has no steady state at all 27 August

Twenty-four points attempted, twelve converged. Both compact dies diverge at both power levels — including at 25 W, where their densities are only 0.517 and 0.648 W/mm², comfortably under the 0.80–0.85 W/mm² grease cliff measured on the x86 die.

floorplandie mm²at 25 W at 40 Woutcome
x86 Skylake-class101.10.247 0.396converges, 39.9 → 52.0 °C
ARM Neoverse V1-class70.20.356 0.570converges, 41.9 → 55.2 °C
ARM Neoverse N2-class48.40.517 0.826no steady state, either power
RISC‑V P670-class38.60.648 1.036no steady state, either power

They fail below the x86 cliff because the cliff is not a property of density alone. A compact die is penalised twice: its power density is higher at the same watts — 2.1× for the N2-class — and the spreading boundary it sees is worse, because that boundary scales with die area (0.553 K/W on the 53 mm² die against 0.325 on the 101 mm² one and 0.108 on the 826 mm² accelerator). Roughly 2.1× the density into roughly 1.8× the resistance is about 3.7× the temperature rise.

Read this as a packaging result, not a verdict on an ISA

It does not say ARM or RISC‑V cores are thermally unviable. It says that at a fixed cooler, shrinking the die is thermally expensive in a way density alone does not capture — and the term that dominates is the area-dependent boundary, which is exactly what a real compact part would cool differently. The transferable lesson is narrower and more useful: any ISA comparison that holds watts fixed has to scale the cooler with die area, or it is measuring the package rather than the architecture.

Taken with the constant-density sweep, the two bracket the answer and fail the original prediction for different reasons — cooler-but-costlier in one, no steady state in the other. That is worth more than a single falsification.

What the published areas changed rebuilt 28 August

Everything above this point was built on floorplans whose block areas came from a power model. A curated pack of published block-level areas — 165 rows transcribed from vendor plates and die analysis, each citing its source — made it possible to check that model against measurements for the first time. The check did not go well for the model, and the rebuilt floorplans overturn one of this handbook’s own results.

The reference core. One core in the pack is fully decomposed: Intel Golden Cove, six published blocks that reconcile to the published core total within 1.35 %. Its sibling Redwood Cove closes to 0.04 %. Two numbers transcribed independently from one plate agreeing that closely is what makes them usable. Areas alone do not fix placement, so the arrangement below is read off the annotated plate and the dimensions are an output of the two together.

Golden Cove to Redwood Cove is a rescale with a published answer, which makes it the error bar on every core built by the same recipe: scaling the template by area ratio lands within 22 % on the worst block and 14 % on average, and the worst block is the L2 — which is exactly what changed between the two parts (2 MB against 1.25 MB). That is the honest accuracy of “scale a core by its area”, measured rather than assumed.

The model’s unit mix disagrees with the one published measurement, and the largest disagreement is a block that is not there. Grouping the model’s units into Golden Cove’s six published blocks, as shares of per-core area:

block groupour modelGolden Cove, publishedratio
frontend — branch, decode, uop cache, L1I10.40 %23.02 %0.45
out-of-order schedule and retire5.13 %18.56 %0.28
load / store with L1D12.64 %14.47 %0.87
FP and vector22.23 %13.84 %1.61
integer execution2.31 %5.64 %0.41
L225.21 %23.11 %1.09
unallocated residual22.08 % 1.35 %16.4

The power model reports a core area its own itemised units fall a fifth short of, and the tiler renders that shortfall as one featureless slab per core — 15.85 mm² of a 101 mm² die, the second largest block on it. A real core, transcribed independently from the same plate as its own total, closes to 1.35 %. Every floorplan metric validated in this handbook was measured on a die a fifth of whose area is a single uniform block.

Three numbers the pack corrects. The vector accelerator was sized by an explicit fudge factor targeting 10 % of die area, and it hits that target; the published plate puts the FMA units at 4.04 % of core, which is 4.8× smaller. The Neoverse V1-to-N1 area ratio was taken from a press claim of “~70 % larger”; the pack’s own rows give 1.80–2.19×, which moves V1 from 29 % smaller than our baseline core to 19 % larger. And the baseline core itself is 1.67× smaller than a real iso-node x86 core — AMD Zen 2, same node class, same 512 KB L2, 3.54 mm² against a modelled 2.12.

The shipped baseline is deliberately not corrected. Every result in this handbook rests on it, and silently recalibrating it would invalidate the back catalogue for the sake of one constant. The corrected core enters as a variant instead, so the size of the correction is measurable rather than asserted.

A defect worth stating plainly, because it changes how the section above reads. The vector width the earlier six floorplans varied was declared and never installed — the constant that sets it is baked in at import and an area file cannot reach it. Measured on the floorplans as built: the vector-to-FPU ratio is 1.981 in every one of them, x86 and ARM and RISC‑V alike. So the registered prediction’s second clause failed with the peak-to-runner-up gap “ordered by nothing” because the input never varied, not because area re-weighting preserves the mix.

The metric that survived phase 1 does not survive the rebuild 28 August

Plateau width against cost was the one predictor left standing — ρ +0.84 across eleven workloads, +1.00 across four floorplans, +1.00 across six. Rebuilding those six on published block areas and holding everything else identical — same density, same margins, same pitch, same burial, same workload — gives:

six floorplans, ρ(plateau, cost)3 K5 K8 K
built from press area ratios+1.00+1.00+0.83
rebuilt on published areas, same density+0.29−0.06−0.29
rebuilt, each part at its own published density+0.73+0.55+0.32

The control is exact: the unchanged x86 die reproduces its old numbers to the last digit, so the only thing that moved is the floorplans. Neither rebuilt arm reproduces +1.0, and a metric of distribution shape swinging from +0.29 to +0.73 on a convention about how watts are handed out is its own indictment.

Why, and it was foreseeable. Every floorplan in the earlier six was a uniform rescale of one unit mix. The only thing that varied was compaction — and plateau width and die size are both monotone in compaction, so they were never independent variables. The rebuild moves block mix and block size independently of die area, and the metric stops predicting. The transfer was a property of that family of re-weightings, not of designs.

What orders cost instead, on the rebuilt dies, is the die’s absolute thermal scale — temperature span at −0.77 to −0.94 in every dataset and both arms. That is the same direction the dropped hot-region-depth metric pointed, and two independent failures agreeing is worth more than either alone. It is also not a validated result: seven quantities were examined here and one of them was registered in advance.

One die per ISA, and they are not equally evidenced 28 August

A per-ISA comparison needs one representative per class. What the public record supports for each is strikingly uneven, and that unevenness is itself a result.

ISAdieareapowerV/Fblock mix
ARMNeoverse V1, 2.52 mm² core + 1 MB L2, 7 nm publishedpublished publishedinherited
x86Golden Cove, 7.123 mm², Intel 7 publishedborrowed nonepublished
RISC‑VXiangShan Kunminghu derivednone noneinherited

ARM is the best-evidenced part in the entire pack. Neoverse V1 is the only row anywhere in it carrying area, power and voltage together — 2.52 mm², 1.2 W, 2.8 GHz, 0.75 V — so it is the only part where area, power and V/F close without an assumption in the chain.

x86 is the best decomposed. Golden Cove is the only core in the pack broken into blocks at all, which is why every other variant’s internal proportions are its proportions, adjusted for cache capacity and vector width. Its power is borrowed: nothing in the pack gives an x86 core its own, so the density used is Tesla’s D1 at 0.62 W/mm² — a same-node logic die, not an x86 part. It happens to land within 4 % of the 0.60 W/mm² this project had been sweeping at anyway, which is reassuring and is not corroboration.

RISC‑V cannot be modelled to the same standard, and that is a property of the field rather than a gap in collection. No published RISC‑V core area exists anywhere in the pack. Three physical layouts do — XuanTie C910, SiFive P870, Ventana Veyron V1 — and only Veyron prints a number: 62.5 mm² for a 16-core cluster on a 5 nm node. Different level of abstraction, different node. There appear to be no photographic RISC‑V die shots in public at all; the silicon rarely gets delidded and imaged the way Intel, AMD and Apple parts do. Anyone quoting a RISC‑V core area from this work is quoting an output of our own model. The one published RISC‑V number that is worth carrying is the cross-check: Veyron V1 at 62.5 mm² beside AMD Bergamo’s 16-core CCD at 69.5 mm² on the same node — 10 % smaller, sixteen cores each way.

And the comparison has to be made at matched die area, which the earlier sweeps were not. Every floorplan above ran at 34 cores, so the dies spanned 62 to 290 mm² — and since absolute thermal scale is what orders cost, a per-ISA claim from that sweep is mostly a claim about die size wearing an architecture’s name. Holding the die at ~100 mm² and letting core count vary (10 Golden Coves, 30 Neoverse V1s, 54 Neoverse N1s, 33 XiangShans) brings the spread to 1.15×, which is what a real product comparison looks like.

The comparison at matched die area, and the block that spoils it 28 August

With one die per ISA and the die area held at ~100 mm², the comparison can finally be made without die size doing the work. Same cooler, same margins, same uniform workload; only the core and how many of them fit.

diecoresdiepowerpeak spanplateaucost at 3 K
x86 Skylake-class (model mix — the control)34 101.2 mm²60.7 W63.1 °C 30.5 K170.491 W
ARM Neoverse N15495.257.1 69.8 °C39.9 K680.732 W
ARM A64FX-class33103.762.2 73.1 °C43.1 K320.367 W
x86 Zen 222108.164.8 86.9 °C57.3 K180.332 W
ARM Neoverse V130109.265.5 87.5 °C58.7 K370.575 W
x86 Golden Cove10~104~63 no steady state

The published-mix dies run 7 to 24 K hotter than the model-mix die at the same area and the same watts, with up to 1.9× the temperature span. That is not an architecture result — it is a result about the power model. Its 22 % unallocated slab was acting as a heat spreader that a real core does not have, and removing it makes every die hotter. Read the other way round: the absolute temperatures in this handbook are optimistic, and the correction is tens of kelvin, not a few.

And the hottest block on every die in this project is an accounting entry. All six dies peak on the same unit — the results broadcast bus — the unmodified baseline included. The power model reports that unit as an area overhead rather than a placed block, and the tiler converts the overhead figure into a rectangle: 0.0019 mm² carrying 0.199 W on the baseline, which is 105 W/mm². Real silicon runs one to three, ten in a bad hotspot.

How much it matters is measurable, and mostly it does not. The bus stands only 0.2–3.9 K above the next block down, so deleting it would move each die’s peak by at most about four kelvin and leave the 24 K spread between dies intact. The exception is the largest core: its area scales with the core, so on Golden Cove the same block carries 1.81 W against the baseline’s 0.199 W, and that is the die with no steady state. Golden Cove’s failure is the artefact, not an architecture result, and no per-ISA thermal ranking should be quoted until a per-block power model replaces this one.

The metric does recover somewhat at matched area, and not enough to rescue it: ρ(plateau, cost) is +0.60 / +0.54 / +0.31 across the six convergent dies at 3, 5 and 8 K — better than the +0.29 / −0.06 / −0.29 it managed when die area was free to vary 4.7×, and still nothing significant at n = 6. Dropping the one legacy model-mix die would lift 3 K to +0.90, and that is exactly the post-hoc fishing this section exists to warn against: the same exclusion decays to +0.50 by 8 K.

Running each part at its own published power density is where the ARM rows finally pay. Every ISA result before this one redistributed one x86 power trace at a common density, which can only ever compare geometry. Six Arm rows carry area and power on the same row, and they say something the geometry cannot: the wide-vector V-class runs at roughly half the power density of the compact N-class — V1 at 0.476 W/mm² against N1 at 0.870.

die at ~100 mm²coresits own density die powerpeakplateaucost at 3 K
x86 Skylake-class (control)340.62062.7 W 64.5 °C170.485 W
ARM Neoverse V1300.476 52.0 W73.5 °C36 0.583 W
ARM A64FX-class (no published density)330.600 62.2 W73.1 °C320.367 W
RISC‑V XiangShan (no published density)330.600 64.4 W77.4 °C310.445 W
x86 Zen 2220.62067.0 W 89.6 °C180.319 W
ARM Neoverse N1540.870 82.8 W92.3 °C71 0.714 W
x86 Golden Cove100.620 no steady state

V1 against N1 is the one comparison here that rests on published numbers at both ends. Same die-area class, same cooler, each at the density its vendor publishes: the wide machine dissipates 31 W less, runs 19 K cooler and is cheaper to cool than the compact one. A wide, low-clocked core spends area to avoid density; a compact one spends density to avoid area, and pays for it thermally at both ends. That is an activity difference, and no amount of area re-weighting at a common density could have produced it — which is precisely why every earlier ISA result here could not see it.

Two cautions that keep this from being a verdict on ARM. The core-internal power shape is still the x86 trace: the pack publishes per-core density and per-block power for nothing, so this is an activity comparison at the die level and a geometry comparison inside the core. And the N1 row takes the compact end of a published range that spans 0.870 to 1.286 W/mm² — a 48 % spread — so the size of the gap is a choice within the evidence, even though its direction is not.

So the honest state of the ISA question is this. The floorplans are now built on published areas and the down-selection is defensible. The comparison between them is not yet, because the peak of every die is set by a mis-placed accounting figure and the absolute temperatures are optimistic by tens of kelvin. That is a smaller, more tractable problem than it looks: it is one block and one line in the tiler, and it is the next thing to fix.

Cost is dominated by how much margin you demand RE-MEASURED 27 August — the relation holds, the numbers are new

Three margin curves. The cost of a rescue rises 30–160× as the demanded target moves a few kelvin, and the knee moves with density — ~94 °C at 1.10 W/mm², ~97 °C at 1.15. It is not an absolute temperature; it tracks the top of the block distribution. Below the knee the target dips into the plateau and cooling anything means cooling everything.

Why this is withdrawn rather than restated

The margin study asks the planner to hold targets of 93–99 °C. On the corrected --spreading boundary the 34-core die at the re-centred densities peaks at 77.5 °C (0.80 W/mm²) and 81.1 °C (0.85), and the liquid arm at 73.0. Every target sits 12–26 K above the peak, so the planner correctly does nothing: all sixteen margin points and both rescue points return “nothing above target; no cooling needed”, zero watts removed, zero blocks engaged. Across the whole catalogue only 17 of 85 points with an MR plan had anything to act on.

So neither density in the struck text exists on the corrected boundary, and neither knee has been measured there. There is no number to substitute — only a re-centred study that has not been run. docs/evidence/catalogue_naming_and_margin_defects.json.

What survives is the mechanism, and it arrived everywhere at once. The third curve was always the uncomfortable one: on a liquid-class sink the die held 93.6 °C unaided and MR engaged zero blocks — better conventional cooling did not make MR more valuable, it made it irrelevant. The spreading correction has now done to the air case exactly what the liquid sink did to the liquid one. On that reading this is not a lost result but the same result generalised: MR’s value is set by how close the die runs to its target, not by how much heat it makes, and correcting the package moved the whole study away from its targets. The liquid figure itself is superseded too — that point now holds 73.0 °C, and still engages zero blocks.

Done the same day — and the answer overturned one of these claims

mr_comparison gained --mr-target-offset-K: the target is now derived from each point's own measured unaided peak instead of stated as an absolute temperature, so the study cannot slide out from under its own targets the next time the boundary moves. The reference is array_idle — the same stack with the laser off — and not the control, which is a different stack and cooler by the passive term; offsetting from the control would re-create this very defect one layer down.

margin demanded, heat removed (W)1 K 2 K3 K5 K 8 K12 Kcost rise
0.80 W/mm², air 0.1440.2860.457 0.7451.7133.453 24.0×
0.85 W/mm², air 0.1440.2860.491 0.7361.6283.428 23.9×
0.80 W/mm², liquid (0.05 K/W) 0.1530.3050.444 0.8502.0453.847 25.1×
blocks the plan must engage 11 36 1232

The knee is the plateau being entered, and you can watch it happen. Up to 2 K of margin the planner hits the target exactly using one block. From 3 K it can no longer hold the target — achieved lags demanded — and the engaged-block count explodes 1 → 3 → 6 → 12 → 32. Past the runner-up, cooling the peak means cooling everything between the target and the peak. It is the same overshoot the tile-pitch and die-average studies found, reached from a third direction.

This overturns the “uncomfortable third curve” above

The struck text said that on a liquid sink the die held 93.6 °C unaided and MR engaged zero blocks — “better conventional cooling did not make MR more valuable, it made it irrelevant.” With a target derived from where the die actually sits, the liquid arm behaves essentially identically to air: 25.1× against 24.0× and 23.9×, the same knee, the same block counts.

The cost-of-margin relation is a property of the die's temperature distribution, not of the cooling class. Both statements are true and they answer different questions. If the requirement is an absolute temperature the die already meets, MR is irrelevant — but that is a fact about the requirement, not about MR or about liquid cooling. The old framing attributed to the cooling class what belonged to the choice of target. docs/evidence/margin_curve_restored.json.

A uniformly loaded accelerator is the wrong target geometry stands temperatures: see the accelerator status in the footer

332 of 367 blocks within the device’s reach of the peak; clipping one buys 0.4% of its capability. All 128 compute tiles span 8.3 K — the array is effectively one thermal object. Unchanged across every leakage assumption we varied.

A realistic kernel overturns that geometry stands temperatures: see the accelerator status in the footer

Uniform activity was a deliberate control — so any hotspot came from geometry rather than from an imbalance assumed into the input — and it is the least favourable input MR could be given. Under a low-occupancy kernel (8 of 128 SMs active, contiguous) on a 700 W part, the plateau collapses 332 → 9 blocks on a die 10 K over its limit.

This also revealed that clip-one gain was the wrong metric here: it stays small because the active tiles are mutually degenerate, while the quantity that matters — how many blocks a rescue must cover — had fallen by 37×.

The binding constraint is lift, not cost reasoning stands — and the constraint has since been lifted

Read this before the argument below — its conclusion has been overtaken

The separation below is sound and the diagnosis was right: the wall was dt_max, not cost. That wall was an unsourced number. The envelope read h_max 10 W/mm² and dt_max 10 K with no provenance, while the device paper's own bench data (Draft 5 §6.4.1) reports 250 W/mm² from a 100 × 100 µm area and a 45 °C reduction — 25× and 4.5× higher. The model was simultaneously pessimistic about capability and optimistic about efficiency (it assumed 20% ASF against 3.5% demonstrated), and the capability half was a hidden ceiling: the planner could never ask for more than 10 K, so any lever needing more was unreachable by assumption.

So “the device ask is one number: get dt_max from 10 K to 13 K” was already satisfied on the bench before it was asked. The catalogue now runs at the demonstrated 250 / 45, and that single change is what opens the top of the laser term's range: across the re-run the laser removes 0.04–124.7 W for 0.3–50.2 K, where the old envelope capped it at 10.

Five accelerator runs exited “iteration limit reached”. Quadrupling the budget moved them 1%. They had not run out of iterations — each had raised its peak by exactly dt_max and stopped. Sweeping the parameter confirmed it against a prediction registered beforehand: the achieved peak tracks uncooled − dt_max precisely, then halts on reaching the target.

So the three candidate constraints separate, and only one binds:

  • Breadth (the plateau) — collapses 332 → 9 under a concentrated kernel. Not binding.
  • Cost (the COP) — oversupplied 34×. Not binding.
  • Depth (dt_max) — needs 13 K, has 10. Binding.

Priced against airflow, MR wins by 34× withdrawn — weak opponent

Holding 98 °C on a 700 W acceleratorcooling diefanMRtotal
more airflow184 CFM369.2 W 205.8 W—575.0 W

Break-even COP 0.0170 against an effective 0.574 — a 33.7× margin, saving 161 W or 28% of system power. The MR arm also runs a cooler die, because clipping the hot blocks suppresses their leakage. The MR plan is flagged non-minimal, so 22.3 W is an upper bound and the true break-even is lower: the error runs in MR’s favour.

What this reframes

Every earlier “MR costs too much” conclusion in this project was measured against a thermal target MR could not reach — not against a cost it could not justify. Efficiency is not the problem. Lift is. The device ask is one number: get dt_max from 10 K to 13 K.

Two caveats that bound this result

It compares MR against fans, which is why it is withdrawn: a 700 W part would not be air-cooled in practice, so the 34× is measured against an opponent nobody would field. Updated 27 August: the second half of this caveat — “the comparison that decides deployment, MR against a cold plate, has not been run and cannot be, as the pipeline stands” — is no longer true. MicrochannelSink is built and anchored on measured data, the GA100 solves on it at 64.0 °C at 700 W, and its channel pump power is reported (0.06 W at 700 W, a floor: manifold, plenum and facility loop are not modelled). The blocking comparison is now runnable and unrun, which makes it a task rather than a limitation.

It is one operating point. The uniformly loaded 700 W case needs dt_max ≥ 30 K and 299 W, 43% of the die. No efficiency rescues that. MR’s case on an accelerator rests specifically on low-occupancy kernels at high TDP.

08 — Workload dependence

The answer changes with what the chip is running

This is not a caveat on the results; it is one of the results. The same die, same power, same cooler gives opposite verdicts depending on the workload’s shape.

What matters is not how much power the workload draws but how concentrated it is, and concentration has two independent axes we can vary:

  • Occupancy — how many compute tiles are active. Real GPU kernels routinely use a fraction of the machine: small grids, tail effects, partitioned inference.
  • Placement — whether the active tiles are physically adjacent. Eight neighbouring tiles pile their heat together; eight scattered across the die each sit in their own cool surroundings. Same occupancy, materially different thermal outcome.

Three kernel shapes are implemented, all real GPU behaviour rather than contrivances: occupancy (N tiles active and boosted, the rest idling), memory-bound (compute stalled, memory interface at full rate), and tensor (power shifted from each tile’s SRAM into its datapath at constant die power).

Only the first produces a hotspot. Memory-bound lands the die at 65 °C with a 171-block plateau — the interface blocks are hot together, not one of them alone. Tensor moves the plateau only 332 → 320: intra-tile concentration barely registers.

The trade that bounds every occupancy result

MR’s leverage peaks where the die is coldest. Idling tiles is what creates the concentration, and it is also what takes the power out. At 2 active tiles the clip-one gain is best in the entire study — 22% of device capability — and the die sits at 72 °C, thirty kelvin below its limit, needing no cooling at all.

Only raising total power gets you both concentration and heat. That is why the accelerator case rests on high-TDP parts running low-occupancy kernels, and not on either condition alone.

One deliberate choice cuts against finding hotspots: within a block class, power is shared equally. Any hotspot therefore comes from geometry rather than from an imbalance we assumed into the input. Real kernels are less even than this, so the results are conservative — and a genuinely skewed activity map is the most promising unexplored route to a stronger accelerator case.

09 — Open gaps

What we cannot yet answer

Ordered by how much each one could move the project’s conclusions.

  1. Which leakage bracket the density ceiling sits on — CLOSED 31 August — it sits on both, and the prediction here was wrong This was listed as the highest-value item outstanding, on the reasoning that the ceiling is decided at 310–330 K and that is where the two ASAP7 brackets — the card as written, and the same card with GIDL disabled — disagree most. The GIDL-off ladder was run: twenty solves. On the uniform arm — the flat-die ceiling, which is the claim that matters — the two brackets are identical: both hold 0.80 and fail 1.00 W/mm². Only the shaped arm's lowest rung changes, and it changes from unconverged to diverged, which is a point becoming decidable rather than a ceiling moving. `[!]` The prediction failed for a reason worth more than the run. It compared leakage levels between the brackets, where the governing mechanism — established in the same section — says compare slopes. In the 316–328 K band the surviving points actually occupy, swapping the old curve for the simulated one changes the feedback gain by 6–14×; swapping GIDL brackets changes it by 1.16–1.27×. One rung moved for the first and none for the second, which is proportionate. So the predictive-PDK GIDL uncertainty does not propagate into the density ceiling, and does not need carrying as a caveat on it.
  2. The cold-zone prize: re-derived, and it came out smaller — CLOSED 31 August — and the recorded ratios were wrong, not merely unreproduced The pair this project had been quoting (34.64 % static, 92.6 % cache share) is now reproduced exactly — all four recorded quantities to the last digit — and reproducing it settled it as a scope error: it sums one core’s blocks against the whole chip’s L3, on the trace’s warm-up slice. The standing guess that it had been measured after leakage feedback converged at the operating temperature is withdrawn: dynamic power does not depend on temperature, and the recorded 2.6062 W is that slice’s Tref dynamic to four decimals. Re-derived on the die power the pipeline actually solves — everything landing on a real floorplan block, over the steady slices — the ratios are 16.0 % static, 38.2 % cache share, and the prize is ~6 % of die power (4.5 % for an L3-only cold die; ~9 % on a McPAT-leaf upper bound that omits core_other, 42 % of on-die leakage). The 10–30 % range is withdrawn at both ends. The 2.2× improvement is untouched, because every conversion multiplies the same saturating factor by a constant — which is exactly why it was the number to lead with.
  3. What the moved ceiling does to the recorded catalogue — still open — but the cheap test named here was run, and it went the other way One rung on one arm is a real move but a small one, and re-running 80,330 solves to chase it is not obviously worth the machine time. The cheap test named here was the clock-headroom search, on the reasoning that a temperature-limited criterion should move more than a divergence test. It moved less. Six cooling points × three curves: the sustainable clock is unchanged at five of six, to the search’s own 0.05 GHz resolution. That prediction is withdrawn. What the run found instead is worth more: the limiter changes at three of six while the clock does not — the old curve ends the search in a thermal runaway, the measured ones at the 100 °C spec limit — which withdraws the handbook’s own claim that a poorly-cooled die “runs away before it reaches spec”. Which part of a leakage curve is load-bearing is a property of the experiment, not of the curve: a fixed-density divergence test never visits the hot tail, because its reported point is one the die survives; a limit search does, because it reads its answer off where survival stops.
  4. MR has never been priced against liquid cooling — narrowed 27 August: the arm now exists, the race has not been run The headline 34× is against fans, and a 700 W accelerator ships on a cold plate. What has changed is that the comparison arm is no longer missing: MicrochannelSink is anchored on a measured reference (1020 W/cm² at <69 °C above inlet, <120 kPa), gives 0.0153 K/W, and lands the GA100 at 64.0 °C at 700 W. It reports pump power rather than omitting it — 0.06 W at 700 W on 1.7e-5 m³/s, which cross-checks against the LCEstimator CDU's per-device nominal of 1.0e-5. That number is a floor, and must be quoted as one: it is the channels alone. Manifold, plenum, facility loop and chiller are still unmodelled, so an MR-versus-cold-plate verdict computed today would still flatter MR. The gap is now a study to run, not a capability to build — and it remains the most important one.
  5. Lift and efficiency are modelled as independent. Real refrigerators lose COP as ΔT rises; MRParams takes lift and efficiency as unrelated numbers. Updated 27 August: the accompanying recommendation — “raise dt_max by 30%” — is obsolete, because the 10 K it was measured against was an unsourced placeholder and the bench demonstrates 45 K. That makes the missing coupling more pressing rather than less: the catalogue now plans against a 4.5× larger ΔT, which is exactly the regime where an unmodelled COP penalty would bite hardest. Nothing that quotes a large ΔT should be treated as priced until this is built.
  6. No per-block power breakdown for the accelerator. Die shots give areas, not dissipation. Which block is hottest — and therefore what MR should aim at — rests on an assumed split. The plateau result does not, but the targeting does.
  7. What clock the laser buys has never been measured — found 27 August The passive term is solid: swapping thermal grease for the GaAs array, with the laser off, is worth +4.0 % of sustainable clock on a poor cooler and +4.7 % on a good one — and it is worth more on a better cooler, which is the opposite of the usual intuition. The laser term next to it is a different matter. Every powered-arm row in the clock study reported exactly the bottom of its own search range, and that turned out to sit on top of five separate defects, each exposed by fixing the one before it — a verdict taken from the wrong place, a plan sized from an assumed sensitivity, a plan with no physical bound on it, cooling that leaked between evaluations without appearing in any recorded field, and a state fix that the codebase's own guard correctly refused. Four are fixed and pinned by tests. The study still cannot produce a number anyone should quote, and the honest position is that the clock question stays open until one survives the consistency check rather than until a fix stops erroring.
  8. No product V/F curve — measured for one part, 27 August — and it carries a lever the model never had The shipped table is not a modern-node curve, and the IRDS replacement is a technology metric that does not survive extrapolation to GPU clocks (it puts a 1.4 GHz part at 0.26 V against a 0.70 V nominal). Comparative results are unaffected — the curve cancels — but no clock ceiling should be quoted from either. And the shipped fit is worse than uncalibrated: it is unphysical. Its α = 0.949 sits below the floor of 1 that Gonzalez et al. (JSSC 1997) set for complete velocity saturation, which is precisely why f(V) = k(V−Vth)α/V turns over and reports a spurious 6.43 GHz ceiling at 9.40 V. Two things follow, and they point in opposite directions. The fit must be redone under α ≥ 1. But the table's 5.0 GHz top is not the defect it looks like — it is a device limit at 1.4 V, since the fit demands 1.82 V for 5.5 GHz and 2.74 V for 6.0, which is oxide breakdown. A vf_clamped verdict is therefore a result: voltage-limited, not thermally limited. The genuinely missing ingredient is voltage per frequency bin from real firmware, and nothing in this repository had it.

    It does now, for one part. Measurements of a Ryzen 9 9950X through AMD's own Curve Optimizer and Curve Shaper — which expose the SMU's internal curve — put 5.0 GHz at 1.08 V where the shipped table demands 1.4 V, and reach 5.63 GHz at 1.35 V. The shipped table therefore overstates dynamic power at 5 GHz by 1.68×, and its ceiling is a property of the table rather than of silicon. One part, enthusiast-press measurement, not a datasheet — product V/F curves are per-part, fused at test, which is precisely why no vendor publishes one.

    And it carries temperature, which no other curve here does. The voltage a part needs at a given frequency rises with temperature, and the sensitivity grows steeply with frequency — roughly doubling between 4.77 and 5.17 GHz. Cooling that part from 90 °C to 40 °C is worth ~8 % of dynamic power at constant clock, or 93 MHz at a fixed voltage ceiling. Every clock result in this project was computed on a temperature-independent curve, so this lever has been absent by construction — the same shape of omission as the unsourced 10 K device ceiling.

  9. Throughput cannot be constrained directly. We can solve for the COP that holds a temperature, but not one that delivers a throughput, which is what a customer actually specifies.
  10. The fan/MR split has never been optimised. The tool exists and has never been run. Every result to date spends on one lever or the other, and the physics says the optimum is interior.
  11. No transient results. Everything is steady-state. Pulsed pre-cooling — aiming the laser at a unit just before it fires — needs a workload trace longer and burstier than the 3.2 ms we have, in which the hot units are essentially flat.
  12. Deep memory stacks hit a solver ceiling at roughly 1.7 M unknowns, not a physical one. See below.

10 — Toolchain

What has to be built

Required to close the gaps above

  • done A cooling specification. Fluid, die footprint, geometry, flow and inlet temperature in; thermal resistance and wall-plug power out, air and liquid alike, invertible for sweeps. Validated against the measured curves where they exist and against a published part where they do not. Its chiller term is what finally makes a liquid loop comparable with an air one rather than free.
  • done A direct-die stack, generated from a specification. No lid, no die attach, the pixel array where the grease was, and the active layer’s burial depth as a parameter. Reachable from every driver that takes --stack, by name or by spec string. A lidded build still reproduces the historical template layer-for-layer, which is what makes the comparison honest rather than a fresh start.
  • done A powered pixel array. Its own die element, its own tile floorplan, negative power, above the silicon — so the burial depth is a real constraint instead of an inert one. Built, tested and measured by examples/mr_placement_probe.py.
  • done The powered array, wired into the study drivers. This was the blocking item on this list; it closed on 26 August. ICEThermalSolver now carries two dies through both the file path and the socket path. The wire order is the reverse of the stack's declaration order — established from the 3D-ICE source, then verified against the one-shot emulator to 5.1e-4 K across a 121 K field. Eight drivers take the array; mr_comparison and clock_headroom emit three arms per point and build a stack per arm, and wiring_for_stack derives placement from the stack, so the flag and the stack cannot disagree silently. The planner optimises over tiles. Wiring it up also surfaced a silent-inertness bug on the newly enabled path: the session branch sent only processor powers and solve_named zero-fills absent elements, so the array would have been present and removed nothing — a wrong answer with no error.
  • done A spreader with overhang. Closed — but not by the route this list proposed, and the difference is worth recording. Linearising the pluggable heat sink into the system matrix is a dead end three times over: 3D-ICE's conventional top heat sink grammar accepts only a heat transfer coefficient and a temperature, the pluggable sink cannot be steady-solved, and its FMU plugins are broken in this build. The analytic boundary route was taken instead — --spreading on eight drivers, with spreading_sink_for_stack as the single join, reproducing docs/evidence/direct_die_overhang.json to the digit. It moved absolute temperatures a long way: the 34-core boundary went 0.0764 → 0.3247 K/W, which is precisely why everything before it had to be re-run.
  • now the top blocker A defensible product V/F curve. The shipped fit is not merely uncalibrated, it is outside its own model's physical range: VF_ALPHA_POWER_FIT has α = 0.949, below the floor of 1 that Gonzalez et al. (JSSC 1997) set for complete velocity saturation. That is why f(V) = k(V−Vth)α/V turns over and reports a spurious 6.43 GHz ceiling at 9.40 V. Note what this does not change: the 5.0 GHz table limit is a device limit at 1.4 V, not a truncated lookup — the fit demands 1.82 V for 5.5 GHz and 2.74 V for 6.0, which is oxide breakdown — so vf_clamped is a result, voltage-limited rather than thermally limited. The missing ingredient is voltage per frequency bin from real firmware, and nothing in this repository has it. Everything downstream of a clock number waits on this, the architecture ladder included.
  • A COP–ΔT coupling in the device model. Currently MRParams takes lift and efficiency as unrelated numbers.
  • Chain the clock search into the break-even solve, so a throughput target can be converted into the temperature it implies and then into a required COP.
  • done Re-run everything through the direct-die stack and the powered array. Complete 27 August: 176 of 180 CPU points and 70 of 72 accelerator points, 714 rows, three arms balanced at 231 each, and zero rows lacking a placement stamp. The gate went first, as this list asked, and it stands at 2 of 4. Two things the re-run itself found are worth more than any single number in it: the grease control has no steady state where the unpowered array does, at 0.85–0.92 W/mm² — 80 rescued operating points before the laser is switched on — and the accelerator's runaway was never a power-map problem but a cold-plate-model one. open One gap remains: the twelve standalone tier screens (results/tiers_*) and the leak_v_exponent sensitivity arms are in no batch script, were not in the re-run plan, and so still exist only at the superseded boundary. See docs/evidence/findings_harvest_correction.json.
  • Validate the clock model too. The published CPU study gives +30.4% clock from cooling alone at a fixed 95 °C limit — four coolers, same silicon. Our own cooling sweep claims a 50× better cooler buys +55%, and that claim has never been checked against anything.
  • Run the hybrid optimiser, and sweep efficiency across it to produce the full (budget, split, throughput, COP) surface rather than points on it.

Solver capacity

Two distinct walls, often conflated:

Speed. Factorisation dominates — 98.9% of a large accelerator run. It scales superlinearly, and the model predicted a 5.64 M-unknown factorisation at 2916 s against 2849 s measured, a 2.3% error over an 8× extrapolation. A GPU direct solver would give an estimated 3.5× on essentially all of it.

Robustness. Deep stacks fail inside SuperLU 4.3’s memory-expansion heuristic at ~1.7 M unknowns — with 629 GB of RAM free and about 2 GB of estimated fill-in. That is a 2011 solver defect, not a capacity limit, and a modern CPU solver fixes it for a fraction of the effort of a CUDA port.

The GPU trigger, as a number

A faster solver only pays in proportion to the number of distinct system matrices a study needs — and workload sweeps need one, while cooling and geometry sweeps need one per point. Break-even is at roughly 140 distinct matrices at accelerator scale, or about three to four full break-even studies.

Go at four or more matrix-diverse studies of that size. No-go while the work is workload sweeps. Two preconditions: group points by matrix first — that alone was worth 10× and cost nothing — and expose the GPUs, which currently report as absent on a node named for six of them.

A note on how this project fails

Worth recording, because it has been consistent. Nearly every apparent physical obstacle here has turned out to be an artefact: a cooling plan sized from a diverging trajectory, a convergence test that got weaker as damping tightened, a session cache constructed inside a loop, a hard-coded timeout read as a hang, an iteration limit read as a device limit, a calibration file path that silently fell back to an assumed model. Each looked like physics and was not.

The practices that catch these — damping verification on every solve, harvesting results from run output rather than transcribing them, recording a prediction before the run, and checking process liveness rather than the absence of a marker — are load-bearing, not bureaucratic. Every published figure in this project that later needed retracting was caught by one of them.

The strongest of them is the newest. Not one of the five defects was found by reading code; every one came from comparing against something external — a second solver path, a lumped estimate, a published part. And in the one case where I reasoned my way to three candidate causes and tested them, all three were wrong and the answer came from measurement. That is the argument for the acceptance gate, and for treating it as a permanent fixture rather than a milestone.

All results are damping-verified coupled 3D-ICE solves with temperature-dependent leakage, harvested from run output rather than transcribed. 863 tests passing, 1 skipped (31 August). `[!]` Every temperature in this document was solved on the pipeline leakage curve — CACTI’s eleven hard-coded numbers, which clamp below 300 K and are ~47× too steep at 500 K. A simulated replacement now exists (see Status, 31 August); it is not the default, deliberately, so that these figures remain the ones the recorded catalogue was produced with. Where it has been spent it moved the cold-zone prize up 2.2× and the flat-die ceiling down one rung. Device and DRAM parameters and the accelerator power split are documented assumptions, not datasheet extractions; accelerator block areas are measured from published die analysis. The V/F curve is worse than an assumption — its fitted α = 0.949 falls below the physical floor of 1, so the curve is outside its own model's range; see “What has to be built”. Nothing here is a product prediction.

Accelerator status, updated 27 August. Their geometry — plateau widths, degeneracy, placement sensitivity — follows from the power map and stands, as it always did. The temperatures now split three ways rather than being withdrawn wholesale:

  • The cooling model that scales with die area now exists and is measured. MicrochannelSink is anchored on a published reference — 1020 W/cm² background flux at <69 °C above inlet and <120 kPa — and gives 0.0153 K/W against the finned water block's 0.0549. Through the full coupled solve the GA100 runs 51.4 °C at 400 W and 64.0 °C at 700 W, converged, peak block MEMCTRL_B0. Those temperatures stand.
  • Every air-cooled accelerator temperature remains withdrawn — and the reason is now known rather than suspected. The old 88.1 °C figures were constant-power solves, taken before leakage feedback was live on the accelerator path. With feedback working, the GA100 at 400 W on 88 CFM air has no steady state at all. The withdrawal was correct and the replacement is RUNAWAY, not a lower number.
  • accelerator_water_envelope.json is superseded: its ~250 W cliff is a property of the water-block model, not of the die. Its measurements stand; its conclusion does not.

CPU results are unaffected throughout.
